Title: FOUR OLD MEN IN THE BASEMENT
AnswerDetails: Real title: Santa Trinita Maestà (Virgin and Child Enthroned, and Prophets), Cimabue, c. 1290–1300, Uffizi Gallery, Florence. Painted for the Vallombrosan church of Santa Trinita in Florence, it has been recorded as Cimabue's since the 16th century. Four Old Testament prophets look out from the arches beneath Mary's towering throne, and the panel now hangs in the Uffizi's first room beside Duccio's and Giotto's enthroned Madonnas.
RealAnswer: Santa Trinita Maestà (Virgin and Child Enthroned, and Prophets)

Title: SHE HAS ACTUAL KNEES
AnswerDetails: Real title: Ognissanti Madonna (Virgin and Child Enthroned, Surrounded by Angels and Saints), Giotto, c. 1300–1305, Uffizi Gallery, Florence. Painted for the church of Ognissanti (All Saints) in Florence. Hung beside the flatter Madonnas of Cimabue and Duccio, Giotto's Virgin has real bulk under her robe, and the kneeling angels at her feet offer vases of roses and lilies.
RealAnswer: Ognissanti Madonna (Virgin and Child Enthroned, Surrounded by Angels and Saints)

Title: SIX ANGELS, ONE ENORMOUS CHAIR
AnswerDetails: Real title: Rucellai Madonna, Duccio di Buoninsegna, 1285, Uffizi Gallery, Florence. Its contract, dated 15 April 1285, is the oldest surviving Italian document of its kind: the Laudesi confraternity ordered it for their chapel in Santa Maria Novella, and it is named after the Rucellai Chapel where it later hung. Vasari credited it to Cimabue, a mistake that went unchallenged for centuries.

Title: SHE WAS IN THE MIDDLE OF A BOOK
AnswerDetails: Real title: Annunciation with St. Margaret and St. Ansanus, Simone Martini and Lippo Memmi, 1333, Uffizi Gallery, Florence. Signed and dated 1333 for the altar of St Ansanus in Siena Cathedral. The angel's greeting, AVE GRATIA PLENA DOMINUS TECUM, runs in raised gold across the background towards Mary, who shrinks back into her cloak; the female saint on the left is named as St Margaret or, in some sources, St Maxima.
RealAnswer: Annunciation with St. Margaret and St. Ansanus

Title: HANDING OVER THE BABY
AnswerDetails: Real title: Presentation in the Temple, Ambrogio Lorenzetti, 1342, Uffizi Gallery, Florence. Signed and dated 1342 for the chapel of San Crescenzio in Siena Cathedral, one of a set of altarpieces on the life of the Virgin by Siena's leading painters. Mary hands her son to the aged Simeon inside a deep, many-columned temple; Ambrogio is last documented in 1348, the year the Black Death reached Siena.

Title: A NUN IN A SHEEPSKIN HOOD
AnswerDetails: Real title: Saint Humility and Scenes from Her Life (the Blessed Humility Altarpiece), Pietro Lorenzetti, c. 1335–1340, Uffizi Gallery, Florence. Saint Humility (1226–1310) was a noblewoman from Faenza who became a nun and founded a Vallombrosan convent in Florence; the small scenes around her show episodes and miracles from her life. The sheepskin over her head is her emblem of humility, and the small kneeling woman at the lower left is probably the patron.
RealAnswer: Saint Humility and Scenes from Her Life (the Blessed Humility Altarpiece)

Title: THREE ARCHES OF GOLD
AnswerDetails: Real title: Triptych with the Virgin and Child between St Matthew and St Nicholas of Bari, Bernardo Daddi, 1328, Uffizi Gallery, Florence. The inscription along the base names the patron, Fra Niccolò de' Mazinghi (hence St Nicholas), the year 1328 and the painter "Bernardus de Florentia". It is Bernardo Daddi's earliest dated work, yet he was confused with Taddeo Gaddi and Nardo di Cione for so long that he was identified as its author only at the end of the 19th century.
RealAnswer: Triptych with the Virgin and Child between St Matthew and St Nicholas of Bari

Title: DOWN AT THE HARBOUR
AnswerDetails: Real title: The Miracle of the Grain Ships and St Nicholas Reviving a Boy (Stories of St Nicholas), Ambrogio Lorenzetti, c. 1330–1335, Uffizi Gallery, Florence. One of a pair of panels on the life of St Nicholas, read from bottom to top: the bishop persuades sailors to share their grain with famine-struck Myra, and their cargo is miraculously refilled; above, he brings back to life a boy killed by the devil disguised as a pilgrim. How the two panels once fitted into an altarpiece is still a mystery, but they show off Ambrogio's gift for storytelling and complicated architecture.
RealAnswer: The Miracle of the Grain Ships and St Nicholas Reviving a Boy (Stories of St Nicholas)

Title: THE ROYAL ROAD TRIP
AnswerDetails: Real title: Adoration of the Magi (the Strozzi Altarpiece), Gentile da Fabriano, 1423, Uffizi Gallery, Florence. Signed and dated May 1423, it was commissioned by the banker Palla Strozzi, one of the richest Florentines of his day. The kings' retinue includes leopards, monkeys, a dromedary and a lion, and the man holding a falcon is often identified as Strozzi himself, perhaps a pun, since a falconer is a strozziere in Tuscan.
RealAnswer: Adoration of the Magi (the Strozzi Altarpiece)

Title: STANDING ON A STRIPED SKY
AnswerDetails: Real title: Coronation of the Virgin, Lorenzo Monaco, 1414, Uffizi Gallery, Florence. Painted by Don Lorenzo, a Camaldolese monk, for the high altar of his own abbey, Santa Maria degli Angeli in Florence. Its inscription says February 1413, which is February 1414 by our calendar, because the Florentine year began on 25 March.

Title: THREE GENERATIONS, ONE THRONE
AnswerDetails: Real title: Virgin and Child with Saint Anne (Sant'Anna Metterza), Masolino and Masaccio, c. 1424–1425, Uffizi Gallery, Florence. A collaboration for the Florentine church of Sant'Ambrogio. The solid, sculptural Virgin and Child and one angel are usually given to the young Masaccio, St Anne and most of the angels to the older Masolino; "Metterza" means "placed third", with Anne set behind her daughter and grandson.
RealAnswer: Virgin and Child with Saint Anne (Sant'Anna Metterza)

Title: THE CROWN NEEDS ONE MORE JEWEL
AnswerDetails: Real title: Coronation of the Virgin, Fra Angelico, 1431–1435, Uffizi Gallery, Florence. Over forty saints and a crowd of dancing, music-making angels surround Mary in heaven. Unusually, Christ is not placing the crown but adding a jewel to it, a detail probably drawn from a vision of the mystic Bridget of Sweden.

Title: LANCES UP, PERSPECTIVE ON
AnswerDetails: Real title: The Battle of San Romano (the Uffizi panel), Paolo Uccello, c. 1435–1440, Uffizi Gallery, Florence. One of three panels celebrating Florence's 1432 victory over Siena at San Romano; the other two are in the National Gallery in London and the Louvre. Here the Sienese commander Bernardino della Carda is knocked from his horse, and the broken lances on the ground are laid out like an exercise in perspective, Uccello's obsession.
RealAnswer: The Battle of San Romano (the Uffizi panel)

Title: ORANGE TREES OVER THE PORCH
AnswerDetails: Real title: Santa Lucia de' Magnoli Altarpiece (Madonna and Child with Saints Francis, John the Baptist, Zenobius and Lucy), Domenico Veneziano, c. 1445, Uffizi Gallery, Florence. Signed OPUS DOMINICI DE VENETIIS, it stood on the high altar of Santa Lucia de' Magnoli in Florence. It is an early "sacra conversazione": four saints share one sunlit portico with Mary instead of standing in separate gold compartments, and its predella panels are now scattered among other museums.
RealAnswer: Santa Lucia de' Magnoli Altarpiece (Madonna and Child with Saints Francis, John the Baptist, Zenobius and Lucy)

Title: ARMS CROSSED, GARDEN WALLED
AnswerDetails: Real title: Annunciation, Alesso Baldovinetti, c. 1457, Uffizi Gallery, Florence. Gabriel greets Mary with his arms crossed over his chest, and behind the arcade lies an enclosed garden, a symbol of Mary's purity taken from the Song of Songs. Baldovinetti later worked alongside the Pollaiolo brothers on the Cardinal of Portugal's chapel at San Miniato al Monte.

Title: THE ANGEL IS GRINNING AT YOU
AnswerDetails: Real title: Madonna and Child with Two Angels (the Lippina), Filippo Lippi, c. 1460–1465, Uffizi Gallery, Florence. Lippi's most famous painting. Tradition identifies the Madonna with Lucrezia Buti, the nun with whom the friar-painter had two children, and the grinning angel has been suggested as their son Filippino, but neither identification is documented.
RealAnswer: Madonna and Child with Two Angels (the Lippina)

Title: THEY ONLY SHOW ONE SIDE
AnswerDetails: Real title: Diptych of the Duke and Duchess of Urbino (Federico da Montefeltro and Battista Sforza), Piero della Francesca, c. 1473–1475, Uffizi Gallery, Florence. Federico is always shown from his left: he had lost his right eye in a tournament. Battista died in 1472, still in her twenties, and her pale complexion may allude to that; on the backs of the panels the couple ride triumphal carts, his drawn by white horses and hers by unicorns.
RealAnswer: Diptych of the Duke and Duchess of Urbino (Federico da Montefeltro and Battista Sforza)

Title: THE FIRST OF SEVEN
AnswerDetails: Real title: Charity, Piero del Pollaiolo, 1469–1470, Uffizi Gallery, Florence. The first of seven Virtues ordered from Piero del Pollaiolo in 1469 for the hall of the Tribunale di Mercanzia, the merchants' court on Piazza della Signoria; the flame between her fingers stands for God's love.

Title: THE STABLE IS A ROMAN RUIN
AnswerDetails: Real title: Adoration of the Magi (tondo), Domenico Ghirlandaio, 1487, Uffizi Gallery, Florence. Dated 1487, this round panel sets the Holy Family among the ruins of an ancient building, a familiar sign of the pagan world giving way to Christianity. Ghirlandaio had studied Roman remains while working in Rome on the walls of the Sistine Chapel, and the kings have laid their crowns at the child's feet.

Title: THE PAINTER SNUCK IN
AnswerDetails: Real title: Coronation of the Virgin (the Maringhi Coronation), Filippo Lippi, c. 1439–1447, Uffizi Gallery, Florence. Painted for the high altar of the Benedictine nuns of Sant'Ambrogio in Florence. Lippi is traditionally said to have painted himself among the onlookers; the kneeling cleric beside an angel's scroll reading IS PERFECIT OPUS ("he made the work") was once taken for the painter too, but is now usually identified as the patron, Francesco Maringhi.
RealAnswer: Coronation of the Virgin (the Maringhi Coronation)

Title: SPOT THE BANKERS
AnswerDetails: Real title: Adoration of the Magi, Sandro Botticelli, 1470–1475, Uffizi Gallery, Florence. Botticelli turned the kings' visit into a parade of Florentine society around the rising Medici; Vasari says the old king at the child's feet is Cosimo the Elder. The young man in the yellow cloak at the far right, looking straight out at us, is usually taken as Botticelli's self-portrait.

Title: NOT IN THE MOOD
AnswerDetails: Real title: Fortitude, Sandro Botticelli, 1470, Uffizi Gallery, Florence. The only one of the seven Virtues for Florence's merchants' court not painted by Piero del Pollaiolo, and Botticelli's earliest documented work. She wears armour over her dress and holds a ruler's baton; the young painter got the job through Tommaso Soderini, thanks to his Medici connections.

Title: NINE GUESTS IN AN ORANGE GROVE
AnswerDetails: Real title: Primavera (Spring), Sandro Botticelli, c. 1480, Uffizi Gallery, Florence. Nine figures from classical myth cross a flowery lawn: at right the west wind Zephyrus seizes the nymph Chloris, who turns into Flora, goddess of spring; Venus stands at the centre beneath a blindfolded Cupid; the three Graces dance, and Mercury closes the scene at left. Its meaning, and whether it celebrates a Medici wedding, is still debated.

Title: BEACH ARRIVAL, NO LUGGAGE
AnswerDetails: Real title: The Birth of Venus, Sandro Botticelli, c. 1485, Uffizi Gallery, Florence. Despite the name it shows Venus arriving on land at Cyprus, blown ashore on a scallop shell by the winds while a young woman waits with a flowered cloak. It is painted on canvas, a cheaper support than panel and often used for pictures for country villas, and was probably made for a member of the Medici family.

Title: SHE IS TAKING NOTES
AnswerDetails: Real title: Madonna of the Magnificat, Sandro Botticelli, c. 1483, Uffizi Gallery, Florence. Guided by her son, Mary writes the hymn that gives the painting its name, "Magnificat anima mea Dominum", while two angels hold a crown over her head. The child's hand rests on a pomegranate, whose red seeds stand for the Passion.

Title: A RING OF ANGELS
AnswerDetails: Real title: Madonna of the Pomegranate, Sandro Botticelli, c. 1487, Uffizi Gallery, Florence. The child grips a split pomegranate, whose red seeds symbolise the blood of the Passion, while angels hold lilies and roses, flowers of the Virgin. One angel's stole carries the words AVE GRATIA PLENA.

Title: HAIR-PULLING CONTEST
AnswerDetails: Real title: Pallas and the Centaur, Sandro Botticelli, c. 1480–1485, Uffizi Gallery, Florence. A young woman with a battle-axe grips a centaur by the hair: reason taming instinct. She is usually read as Pallas Athena, though some see Camilla, a warrior virgin; her dress is patterned with the Medici three-ring emblem, and the picture belonged to Lorenzo di Pierfrancesco de' Medici, perhaps for his marriage in 1482.

Title: HE ARRIVES, SHE BENDS
AnswerDetails: Real title: Cestello Annunciation, Sandro Botticelli, 1489–1490, Uffizi Gallery, Florence. Commissioned in 1489 by the moneychanger Benedetto Guardi for his family chapel in the church of Cestello (Santa Maria Maddalena in Borgo Pinti), Florence. The bare room and the almost dancing gestures of Gabriel and Mary are often linked to the austere mood of Savonarola's sermons.

Title: THE KING HAS DONKEY EARS
AnswerDetails: Real title: Calumny of Apelles, Sandro Botticelli, c. 1495, Uffizi Gallery, Florence. Botticelli's recreation of a lost painting by the ancient Greek artist Apelles, known only from a description by the writer Lucian. Read from right to left: a king with ass's ears, advised by Ignorance and Suspicion, judges a man dragged in by the hair by Calumny, while naked Truth at the far left points to heaven.

Title: EVERYONE WANTS A LOOK
AnswerDetails: Real title: Adoration of the Magi, Filippino Lippi, 1496, Uffizi Gallery, Florence. Signed and dated 29 March 1496 by Filippino Lippi, son of Filippo and once Botticelli's pupil. It was painted for the monks of San Donato a Scopeto, and the kneeling man with an astrolabe is thought to be Pier Francesco de' Medici.

Title: WHO PAINTED THE ANGEL?
AnswerDetails: Real title: The Baptism of Christ, Andrea del Verrocchio and Leonardo da Vinci, c. 1470–1475, Uffizi Gallery, Florence. A product of Verrocchio's workshop. Vasari tells that the young Leonardo painted the angel on the left so well that Verrocchio swore never to touch paint again; the vow is legend, but Leonardo's hand in that angel and in parts of the landscape is generally accepted.

Title: A GARDEN DELIVERY
AnswerDetails: Real title: Annunciation, Leonardo da Vinci, c. 1472, Uffizi Gallery, Florence. One of Leonardo's earliest paintings, made while he was still working in Verrocchio's workshop. Gabriel's wings were modelled on a bird of prey's and were later lengthened by another hand, and the panel was credited to Ghirlandaio until scholars gave it to Leonardo in the 19th century.

Title: A CROWD IN BROWN
AnswerDetails: Real title: Adoration of the Magi, Leonardo da Vinci, c. 1481–1482, Uffizi Gallery, Florence. Commissioned in 1481 by the Augustinian monks of San Donato a Scopeto, it was left unfinished when Leonardo moved to Milan; what we see is essentially the underdrawing and first layers. A restoration completed in 2017 cleared away darkened varnish and brought back many details; the image here shows it before that cleaning.

Title: UNDER THE PORCH, IN SILENCE
AnswerDetails: Real title: Pietà, Perugino, c. 1493–1496, Uffizi Gallery, Florence. Mary holds her dead son across her lap under a plain stone portico, with mourners on either side, in Perugino's calm, symmetrical manner. He was one of the most sought-after painters in Italy at the time, and the young Raphael is traditionally said to have trained with him.

Title: A ROUND PICTURE, MUSCLES INCLUDED
AnswerDetails: Real title: Doni Tondo (Holy Family), Michelangelo, 1505–1506, Uffizi Gallery, Florence. Painted for the merchant Agnolo Doni, around his marriage to Maddalena Strozzi in 1504 and the birth of their first child; it is the only finished panel painting by Michelangelo to survive. The nude youths behind the low wall are usually read as the pagan world before Christ.

Title: TWO BOYS AND A BIRD
AnswerDetails: Real title: Madonna of the Goldfinch (Madonna del Cardellino), Raphael, c. 1505–1506, Uffizi Gallery, Florence. Painted in Florence for the wedding of Lorenzo Nasi in February 1506. When the Nasi house collapsed in a landslide in 1547 the panel broke into seventeen pieces; it was pieced back together, and a ten-year restoration finished in 2008 brought its colours back.
RealAnswer: Madonna of the Goldfinch (Madonna del Cardellino)

Title: PAGEBOY HAIR, PAINTER'S CAP
AnswerDetails: Real title: Self-portrait, Raphael, c. 1506, Uffizi Gallery, Florence. Raphael at about 23, recognised by comparison with his likeness in the School of Athens in the Vatican. It belongs to the Uffizi's celebrated collection of artists' self-portraits, begun by Cardinal Leopoldo de' Medici in the 17th century.

Title: MORNING HUG
AnswerDetails: Real title: Visitation, Mariotto Albertinelli, 1503, Uffizi Gallery, Florence. Mary greets her relative Elizabeth, the future mother of John the Baptist, under a stone arch carved with the date 1503. Albertinelli shared a workshop with Fra Bartolomeo and, according to Vasari, once gave up painting for a while to run a tavern.

Title: MONSTERS ON THE PEDESTAL
AnswerDetails: Real title: Madonna of the Harpies, Andrea del Sarto, 1517, Uffizi Gallery, Florence. Signed and dated 1517 for the nuns of San Francesco de' Macci in Florence. The nickname comes from the small winged creatures carved on Mary's pedestal, read as harpies, though they may be the locusts of the Book of Revelation.

Title: MONSTER DAY AT THE BEACH
AnswerDetails: Real title: Perseus Freeing Andromeda, Piero di Cosimo, c. 1510–1515, Uffizi Gallery, Florence. Perseus appears three times: swooping in on winged sandals, fighting the sea monster at the centre, and celebrating with Andromeda and the crowd. Vasari described Piero di Cosimo as a famous eccentric who lived on eggs, hard-boiled fifty at a time.

Title: VERY LARGE SHEPHERDS
AnswerDetails: Real title: Portinari Altarpiece (Portinari Triptych), Hugo van der Goes, c. 1475–1476, Uffizi Gallery, Florence. Commissioned in Bruges by Tommaso Portinari, the Medici bank's agent there, and shipped to Florence in 1483 for the church of Sant'Egidio, where he and his family appear on the wings. Its rough, sharply observed shepherds made a deep impression on Florentine painters such as Ghirlandaio.

Title: THREE LITTLE SCENES
AnswerDetails: Real title: The Uffizi Triptych (Ascension, Adoration of the Magi, Circumcision), Andrea Mantegna, c. 1460–1465, Uffizi Gallery, Florence. The three panels were put together in a 19th-century frame, so the triptych itself is a modern arrangement. They probably come from a cycle Ludovico Gonzaga commissioned from Mantegna for the chapel of the Castle of St George in Mantua, which was later lost to rebuilding.
RealAnswer: The Uffizi Triptych (Ascension, Adoration of the Magi, Circumcision)

Title: A TERRACE FULL OF RIDDLES
AnswerDetails: Real title: Sacred Allegory (Holy Allegory), Giovanni Bellini, c. 1490–1500, Uffizi Gallery, Florence. One of the most puzzling pictures of the Renaissance: saints, children and the Madonna gather on a marble terrace beside still water, and no one agrees what it means. Suggestions range from a vision of Paradise to an allegory centred on the child on the cushion, possibly Jesus.

Title: A TEST AT THE ROYAL PICNIC
AnswerDetails: Real title: Moses Undergoing Trial by Fire, Giorgione (attributed), c. 1502–1505, Uffizi Gallery, Florence. From a Jewish legend, not the Bible: Pharaoh tests the infant Moses with a dish of gold and a dish of hot coals, and the child chooses the coals. Usually attributed to the young Giorgione, with some figures possibly by an assistant; its companion piece, the Judgement of Solomon, is also in the Uffizi.

Title: KINGS AMONG THE RUINS
AnswerDetails: Real title: Adoration of the Magi, Albrecht Dürer, 1504, Uffizi Gallery, Florence. Painted in Nuremberg in 1504, between Dürer's two journeys to Italy, it joins northern detail to Italian perspective and classical ruins. It was made for Frederick the Wise of Saxony and reached Florence in 1603, when Emperor Rudolf II exchanged it for a painting by Fra Bartolomeo.

Title: SNACK TIME IN THE GARDEN
AnswerDetails: Real title: Adam and Eve, Lucas Cranach the Elder, 1528, Uffizi Gallery, Florence. A pair of tall, narrow panels by the painter who ran one of the busiest workshops in Germany and returned to this subject many times. They were in the Tuscan grand dukes' collections by 1688 and have been in the Uffizi since the early 18th century.

Title: THE KING'S MAN
AnswerDetails: Real title: Portrait of Sir Richard Southwell, Hans Holbein the Younger, 1536, Uffizi Gallery, Florence. Southwell was a privy councillor of Henry VIII; the inscription gives the date, 10 July in the 28th year of Henry's reign (1536), and the sitter's age, 33. Grand Duke Cosimo II asked Thomas Howard, Earl of Arundel, for it in 1620 to fill a gap in the Medici collections.

Title: BLOSSOMS IN HAND
AnswerDetails: Real title: Flora, Titian, c. 1517, Uffizi Gallery, Florence. A young woman in an antique-style robe holds out roses, violets and jasmine. She has been identified as Flora, goddess of spring, though some read her as a bride or a courtesan; her copper-blonde hair is the shade later called "Titian red".

Title: THE DOG IS ASLEEP
AnswerDetails: Real title: Venus of Urbino, Titian, 1538, Uffizi Gallery, Florence. Bought in 1538 by Guidobaldo della Rovere, soon Duke of Urbino, who in a letter called it simply "the nude woman". Behind her, maids search a chest for her clothes, and the sleeping dog is a sign of fidelity; Mark Twain called it the foulest picture the world possesses.

Title: ARMOUR POLISHED, BATON READY
AnswerDetails: Real title: Portrait of Francesco Maria della Rovere, Duke of Urbino, Titian, c. 1536–1538, Uffizi Gallery, Florence. The duke, captain general of Venice's armies, sent his parade armour to Titian so it could be painted exactly, then asked for it back in the summer of 1536. Titian's matching portrait of his wife, Eleonora Gonzaga, is also in the Uffizi.
RealAnswer: Portrait of Francesco Maria della Rovere, Duke of Urbino

Title: HE HAS A NEW HAIRDRESSER
AnswerDetails: Real title: Man with a Monkey, Annibale Carracci (attributed), c. 1590–1591, Uffizi Gallery, Florence. A Barbary ape picks through the hair of an amused young man, a slice of everyday life that was rare in painting at the time. It is usually given to Annibale Carracci, though some critics have proposed Titian or Tintoretto; Annibale and his brother Agostino founded an academy in Bologna to lead painting away from Mannerism.

Title: TINY HANDS, BIG INSTRUMENT
AnswerDetails: Real title: Musician Angel (Angel Playing the Lute), Rosso Fiorentino, 1521, Uffizi Gallery, Florence. Probably a fragment of a lost altarpiece, where the little angel would have sat at the foot of a larger scene. Infrared studies found part of a building, and Rosso's name with the date 1521, under the dark background, which was added later.

Title: BLUE BACKGROUND, BEST DRESS
AnswerDetails: Real title: Portrait of Eleonora di Toledo with her son Giovanni, Bronzino, c. 1545, Uffizi Gallery, Florence. Eleonora, the Spanish-born wife of Duke Cosimo I de' Medici, with their second son Giovanni. The blue is lapis lazuli, the costliest pigment, usually kept for the Virgin's robe; the old story that she was buried in this very dress has been disproved.
RealAnswer: Portrait of Eleonora di Toledo with her son Giovanni

Title: A BOOK, A CHAIN, A STEADY GAZE
AnswerDetails: Real title: Portrait of Lucrezia Panciatichi, Bronzino, 1541–1545, Uffizi Gallery, Florence. Lucrezia Pucci, wife of the banker Bartolomeo Panciatichi, whose portrait by Bronzino also hangs in the Uffizi. Her gold chain is inscribed AMOUR DURE SANS FIN, "love lasts without end".

Title: ELEGANCE, EXTENDED
AnswerDetails: Real title: Madonna with the Long Neck, Parmigianino, 1534–1540, Uffizi Gallery, Florence. Commissioned in 1534 by Elena Baiardi for a chapel in Parma, it was still unfinished when Parmigianino died in 1540, as an inscription at the foot of the column admits; the colonnade behind has only one complete column. Its stretched proportions make it a textbook example of Mannerism.

Title: A GLASS FOR YOU?
AnswerDetails: Real title: Bacchus, Caravaggio, c. 1598, Uffizi Gallery, Florence. The young god offers a glass of red wine with his left hand, perhaps because Caravaggio painted his model in a mirror, and the fruit bowl is a still life in its own right. The picture lay forgotten until it was found in the Uffizi's storerooms in the early 20th century.

Title: A SHIELD WITH A SCREAM
AnswerDetails: Real title: Medusa, Caravaggio, c. 1597, Uffizi Gallery, Florence. Painted on a convex wooden parade shield, the second of Caravaggio's two versions, commissioned by Cardinal Francesco del Monte as a gift for Grand Duke Ferdinando I de' Medici. The screaming face is often said to be Caravaggio's own.

Title: SAVED BY A FIRM GRIP
AnswerDetails: Real title: Sacrifice of Isaac, Caravaggio, c. 1603, Uffizi Gallery, Florence. Painted for Cardinal Maffeo Barberini, the future Pope Urban VIII. At the last moment an angel grips Abraham's wrist and points to a ram to be sacrificed instead, while Isaac cries out.

Title: THE MAID HOLDS HIM DOWN
AnswerDetails: Real title: Judith Slaying Holofernes, Artemisia Gentileschi, c. 1620, Uffizi Gallery, Florence. Finished in Rome around 1620, after Artemisia's seven years in Florence, for Grand Duke Cosimo II de' Medici; she was paid only after long delays, and with help from her friend Galileo. In 1616 she had become the first woman admitted to Florence's Accademia delle Arti del Disegno.

Title: FRUIT FROM A FRIENDLY TREE
AnswerDetails: Real title: Rest on the Flight into Egypt with St Francis, Correggio, c. 1520, Uffizi Gallery, Florence. Commissioned around 1520 by the jurist Francesco Munari for his family chapel in the church of San Francesco in Correggio. It follows an apocryphal gospel in which a date palm bends down to feed the Holy Family; St Francis, the patron's namesake, joins them although he lived twelve centuries later.
RealAnswer: Rest on the Flight into Egypt with St Francis
